entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.16.6-Job.9.6">Job 16:6-9   6</reference>  If I speak, my pain is not soothed; <div eID="gen7527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7528" type="x-p"/> And if I forbear, what alleviation do I experience?   7  Nevertheless now hath He exhausted me; <div eID="gen7528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7529" type="x-p"/> Thou hast desolated all my household,   8  And Thou filledst me with wrinkles - for a witness was it, <div eID="gen7529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7530" type="x-p"/> And my leanness rose up against me <div eID="gen7530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7531" type="x-p"/> Complaining to my face.   9  His wrath tore me, and made war upon me; <div eID="gen7531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7532" type="x-p"/> He hath gnashed upon me with His teeth, <div eID="gen7532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7533" type="x-p"/> As mine enemy He sharpeneth His eyes against me. אם stands with the cohortative in the hypothetical antecedent clause <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.16.6">Job 16:6</reference></hi>, and in 6 <hi type="italic">b </hi>the cohortative stands alone as <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">Psa 73:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference>, which is more usual, and more in accordance with the meaning which the cohortative has in itself, Nägelsbach, §89, 3. The interrogative, What goes from me? is equivalent to, what (= nothing) of pain forsakes me. The subject of the assertion which follows (<reference osisRef="Job.16.7">Job 16:7</reference>) is not the pain - Aben-Ezra thinks even that this is addressed in v. 7 <hi type="italic">b - </hi>still less Eliphaz, whom some think, particularly on account of the sharp expressions which follow, must be understood, but God, whose wrath Job regards as the cause of his suffering, and feels as the most intolerable part of it. A strained connection is obtained by taking אך either in an affirmative sense (Ew.: surely), as <reference osisRef="Job.18.21">Job 18:21</reference>, or in a restrictive sense: only (= entirely) He has now exhausted me (Hirz., Hahn, also Schlottm.: only I feel myself oppressed, at least to express this), by which interpretation the עתּה, which stands between אך and the verb, is in the way. We render it therefore in the adversative signification: nevertheless (<hi type="italic">verum tamen</hi>) now he seeks neither by speaking to alleviate his pain, nor by silence to control himself; God has placed him in a condition in which all his strength is exhausted. He is absolutely incapable of offering any resistance to his pain, and care has also been taken that no solacing word shall come to him from any quarter: Thou hast made all my society desolate (Carey: all my clan); עדה of the household, as in Job 15:34. Jerome: <hi type="italic">in nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei</hi> (כל אברי, as explained by the Jewish expositors, e.g., Ralbag), as though the human organism could be called עדה. Hahn: Thou hast destroyed all my testimony, which must have been אדתי (from עוּד, whereas עדה, from ועד, has a changeable <hi type="italic">Ssere</hi>). He means to say that he stands entirely alone, and neither sees nor hears anything consolatory, for he does not count his wife. He is therefore completely shut up to himself; God has shrivelled him up; and this suffering form to which God has reduced him, is become an evidence, i.e., for himself and for others, as the three friends, an accusation <hi type="italic">de facto</hi>, which puts him down as a sinner, although his self-consciousness testifies the opposite to him.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.16.12-Job.14.12">Job 16:12-14 12</reference>  I was at ease, but He hath broken me in pieces; <div eID="gen7539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7540" type="x-p"/> And He hath taken me by the neck and shaken me to pieces, <div eID="gen7540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7541" type="x-p"/> And set me up for a mark for himself. 13  His arrows whistled about me; <div eID="gen7541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7542" type="x-p"/> He pierced my reins without sparing; <div eID="gen7542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7543" type="x-p"/> He poured out my gall upon the ground. 14  He brake through me breach upon breach, <div eID="gen7543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7544" type="x-p"/> He ran upon me like a mighty warrior. <div eID="gen7544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7545" type="x-p"/> He was prosperous and contented, when all at once God began to be enraged against him; the intensive form פּרפּר (Arab. <hi type="italic">farfara</hi>) signifies to break up entirely, crush, crumble in pieces (<hi type="italic">Hithpo.</hi> to become fragile, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.19">Isa 24:19</reference>); the corresponding intensive form פּצפּץ (from פּצץ, Arab. <hi type="italic">fḍḍ</hi>, cogn. נפץ), to beat in pieces (<hi type="italic">Polel</hi> of a hammer, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.29">Jer 23:29</reference>), to dash to pieces: taking him by the neck, God raised him on high in order to dash him to the ground with all His might. מטּרה (from נטר, τηρεῖν, like σκοπός from σκέπτισθαι) is the target, as in the similar passage, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.12">Lam 3:12</reference>, distinct from מפגּע, <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>, object of attack and point of attack: God has set me up for a target for himself, in order as it were to try what He and His arrows can do. Accordingly רבּיו (from רבב = רבה, רמה, <hi type="italic">jacere</hi>) signifies not: His archers (although this figure would be admissible after <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.12">Job 19:12</reference>, and the form after the analogy of רב, רע, etc., is naturally taken as a substantival adj.), but, especially since God appears directly as the actor: His arrows (= הצּיו, <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">Job 6:4</reference>), from רב, formed after the analogy of בּז, מס, etc., according to which it is translated by lxx, Targ., Jer., while most of the Jewish expositors, referring to <reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">Jer 50:29</reference> (where we need not, with Böttch., point רבים, and here רביו), interpret by מורי החצים. S. 268). It is difficult to conceive what is here said;<note placement="foot">The emptying of the gall takes place if the gall-bladder or any of its ducts are torn; but how the gall itself (without assuming some morbid condition) can flow outwardly, even with a severe wound, is a difficult question, with which only those who have no appreciation of the standpoint of imagery and poetry will distress themselves. [On the ”spilling of the gall” or “bursting of the gall-bladder” among the Arabs, as the working of violent and painful emotions, vid., <hi type="italic">Zeitschr. der deutschen morgenländ</hi>. Gesellsch. Bd. xvi. S. 586, Z. 16ff. - Fl.]</note> it is, moreover, not meant to be understood strictly according to the sense: the divine arrows, which are only an image for divinely decreed sufferings, pressed into his inward parts, and wounded the noblest organs of his nature. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.16.15-Job.17.15">Job 16:15-17 15</reference>  I sewed sackcloth upon my skin, <div eID="gen7546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7547" type="x-p"/> And defiled my horn with dust. 16  My face is exceeding red with weeping, <div eID="gen7547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7548" type="x-p"/> And on mine eyelids is the shadow of death, 17  Although there is no wrong in my hand, <div eID="gen7548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7549" type="x-p"/> And my prayer is pure. <div eID="gen7549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7550" type="x-p"/> Coarse-haired cloth is the recognised clothing which the deeply sorrowful puts on, ἱμάτιον στενοχωρίας καὶ πένθους, as the Greek expositors remark. Job does not say of it that he put it on or slung it round him, but that he sewed it upon his naked body; and this is to be attributed to the hideous distortion of the body by elephantiasis, which will not admit of the use of the ordinary form of clothes. For the same reason he also uses, not עורי, but גּלדּי, which signifies either the scurfy scaly surface (as גּלד and הנליד in Talmudic of the scab of a healing wound, but also occurring e.g., of the bedaggled edge of clothes when it has become dry), or scornfully describes the skin as already almost dead; for the healthy skin is called עזר, גּלד, on the other hand, βύρσα (lxx), hide (esp. when removed from the body), Talm. e.g., sole-leather. According to this idea, in the lofty consciousness of his innocence, Job calls upon the earth not to suck in his blood as of one innocently slain, but to let it lie bare, thereby showing that it must be first of all avenged ere the earth can take it up;<note placement="foot">As, according to the tradition, it is said to have been impossible to remove the stain of the blood of Zachariah the son of Jehoiada, who was murdered in the court of the temple, until it was removed by the destruction of the temple itself.</note> and for his cry, i.e., the cry (זעקתי to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Gen.4.10">Gen 4:10</reference>) proceeding from his blood as from his poured-out soul, he desires that it may urge its way unhindered and unstilled towards heaven without finding a place of rest (Symm. στάσις).
